plan: Hard vocabulary (hagiography), sentence function, explanation-revision structure, gap-over-time data, a weed/size causal inference, quotation-plus-appositive punctuation; S007-03 resubmitted with a near-miss distractor.

passages.title: Senator biography
passages.text: Critics had expected the biography to be a ______, given that its author had worked for the senator for twenty years. Instead, the book is unsparing in its account of the senator's failures, devoting entire chapters to decisions the author calls disastrous.

passages.title: Night heat
passages.text: Most studies of urban heat have focused on daytime temperatures. Yet for human health, nighttime temperatures may matter more, because the body recovers from daytime heat stress only when temperatures fall after dark. Climatologist Kofi Asante's measurements show that in dense neighborhoods, pavement and buildings release stored heat at night, keeping nights as much as 5°C warmer than in nearby parks.

passages.title: Salmon decline
passages.text: For decades, the decline of salmon in the Varna River was blamed on overfishing. When fishing limits were tightened in the 1990s, however, salmon numbers kept falling. Biologist Mara Lindqvist then noticed that the decline closely tracked the construction of small dams on the river's tributaries, which block salmon from reaching their spawning streams. Since several of those dams were removed in 2015, salmon counts in the affected tributaries have tripled.

passages.title: Nesting success
passages.text:
Researchers recorded the percentage of nests that produced at least one fledgling for two bird species at a wetland preserve.
Year | Species A | Species B
2015 | 70% | 40%
2018 | 66% | 52%
2021 | 63% | 60%
The researchers noted that the gap between the two species' nesting success narrowed considerably over this period.

passages.title: Cotton pests
passages.text: In laboratory trials, a pest-resistant cotton strain reduced caterpillar damage by 90 percent, but in farm trials the reduction was only 40 percent. The researchers found that on farms, caterpillars often fed first on weeds growing between the rows of cotton, which let them grow larger before moving onto the cotton plants, and larger caterpillars are much less affected by the strain's toxin. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Poet phrase
passages.text: In a 1962 interview, the poet described her hometown as ______ a phrase that later became the title of her best-known collection.

passages.title: Sample collection
passages.text: Having spent three years collecting soil samples from more than two hundred farms, ______ for the care with which she documented each site.

passages.title: Bus routes
passages.text: The committee's report found no evidence that the new bus routes had reduced overall ridership. ______ it recommended that the city restore two of the old routes, citing complaints from riders who now faced much longer walks to their stops.

passages.title: Tide gauge notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A tide gauge records the height of the sea surface at one location.
• Readings are usually taken every few minutes.
• Long records from tide gauges help scientists track changes in average sea level.
• The gauge at Port Ellery has operated continuously since 1904.

passages.title: Base rates
passages.text: In a survey of people who had developed a certain digestive condition, 80% reported regularly drinking a popular brand of sparkling water. A commentator cited this figure as evidence that the drink may cause the condition. But in the population as a whole, about 80% of people also report regularly drinking that brand, which suggests that ______

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: Instead, the book is unsparing in its account of the senator's failures
candidates.explanation: "Instead" contrasts the expectation with an unsparing, critical book, so critics expected an uncritically admiring biography: a "hagiography."

B.rationale: A polemic attacks its subject; critics expected the opposite from a longtime employee.

C.rationale: A chronicle is a neutral record; an unsparing account would not contradict that expectation.

D.rationale: A satire mocks its subject, which a loyal former employee would be unlikely to write.

hints: What does "Instead" tell you about the expectation?
What would a longtime employee be expected to write?
candidates.remember: Use the contrast word to reverse the clue.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a finding that the measurements in the third sentence contradict.
choices.B: It explains why the kind of measurement described in the third sentence matters.
choices.C: It summarizes the methods Asante used to measure temperatures in the city.
choices.D: It gives an example of the daytime studies mentioned in the first sentence.

candidates.explanation: The first sentence notes a daytime focus; the second argues that nights matter more for health; the third reports nighttime measurements. The second sentence thus justifies the importance of the third's focus.

A.rationale: Asante's findings are consistent with the second sentence's concern.

C.rationale: Methods are not described in the second sentence.

D.rationale: It shifts attention from daytime to nighttime rather than giving an example.

hints: How does the second sentence relate to the first and third?

strategy.explanation: Describe each sentence's role, then match.

candidates.remember: A "Yet" sentence often sets up why what follows matters.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a problem, proposes a single solution, and then explains why that solution failed.
choices.B: It compares two rivers' salmon populations and explains why their outcomes have differed.
choices.C: It gives an explanation, notes evidence against it, offers another, and reports support for the second.
choices.D: It presents a hypothesis about salmon and then explains why it cannot yet be tested.

candidates.evidence: When fishing limits were tightened in the 1990s, however, salmon numbers kept falling.
candidates.explanation: Overfishing (explanation) → numbers fell despite limits (evidence against) → dams (alternative) → counts tripled after removal (support).

A.rationale: Dam removal worked; nothing is described as failing at the end.

D.rationale: The dam hypothesis was in effect tested by the 2015 removals.

strategy.explanation: Outline the sentences in a few words each.

candidates.remember: Structure questions reward labeling each sentence's job.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to illustrate the researchers' observation?

choices.A: Species A had a higher nesting success rate than Species B in each of the years shown.
choices.B: Species B's nesting success rose by a total of 20 percentage points from 2015 to 2021.
choices.C: In 2018, Species A's nesting success was 66%, while Species B's success was 52%.
choices.D: Species A fell from 70% to 63% and Species B rose from 40% to 60%, cutting a 30-point gap to 3.

candidates.evidence: the gap between the two species' nesting success narrowed considerably
candidates.explanation: A narrowing gap requires the difference at the start and the end: 30 points in 2015 (70 − 40) and 3 in 2021 (63 − 60).

A.rationale: Being higher every year does not show the gap shrinking.

B.rationale: This gives one species' change, not the gap between them.

C.rationale: A single year cannot show change over time.

hints: What two numbers define a gap narrowing?

strategy.explanation: Turn the observation into what must be shown.

candidates.remember: A change in a gap needs the gap at two times.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: removing the weeds between rows could make the strain more effective on farms.
choices.B: the strain's toxin breaks down quickly when cotton is grown in field conditions.
choices.C: laboratory trials tend to overstate how much damage small caterpillars cause.
choices.D: caterpillars on farms prefer weeds to cotton plants at every stage of growth.

candidates.evidence: which let them grow larger before moving onto the cotton plants
candidates.explanation: Weeds let caterpillars grow large enough to resist the toxin before reaching the cotton. Removing the weeds would remove that head start.

B.rationale: The text explains the gap through caterpillar size, not toxin breakdown.

C.rationale: The lab trials measured the strain's effect, not overstated damage.

D.rationale: They move onto cotton after growing; "every stage" goes too far.

hints: What do the weeds allow the caterpillars to do?

strategy.explanation: Predict the fix implied by the cause.

candidates.remember: If a cause is identified, the logical step addresses it.

candidates.subskill: Punctuating a quotation followed by an appositive
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: "a lantern left on in the rain"
choices.B: "a lantern left on in the rain;"
choices.C: "a lantern left on in the rain,"
choices.D: "a lantern, left on in the rain,"

candidates.evidence: a phrase that later became the title
candidates.explanation: "A phrase that later became ..." renames the quoted words, so it is set off by a comma, which goes inside the closing quotation mark.

A.rationale: Without a comma, the quotation runs directly into the appositive "a phrase ..."

B.rationale: A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, but "a phrase that ..." is not one.

D.rationale: The comma after "lantern" breaks up the quoted phrase.

hints: Is what follows a complete clause?

strategy.explanation: Check what kind of element follows the quotation.

candidates.remember: An appositive after a quotation is set off with a comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.B: Ruiz's methods were praised by the grant committee
choices.C: praise from the grant committee was given to Ruiz
choices.D: Ruiz earned the grant committee's praise

candidates.evidence: Having spent three years collecting soil samples
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase describes the person who collected samples, so "Ruiz" must come right after the comma as the subject.

A.rationale: The committee did not spend three years collecting samples.

B.rationale: The methods did not collect the samples; Ruiz did.

hints: Who spent three years collecting samples?

strategy.explanation: Ask who the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier attaches to the subject after the comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: found no evidence that the new bus routes had reduced overall ridership
candidates.explanation: Finding no ridership loss would argue against change, yet the committee recommends restoring routes anyway, for another reason. "Still" marks that concession.

A.rationale: The recommendation does not follow from finding no drop in ridership; it comes despite it.

C.rationale: The recommendation is not an example of the finding.

D.rationale: The recommendation is not similar to the finding.

hints: Does the finding support or undercut the recommendation?
candidates.remember: Use a concession transition when a conclusion comes despite a fact.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain to an audience unfamiliar with tide gauges why long tide-gauge records are valuable. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: A tide gauge records sea height at one place, and long records help scientists track average sea level.
choices.B: The tide gauge at Port Ellery has been recording sea-surface height continuously since 1904.
choices.C: Tide gauges usually take readings of the sea surface every few minutes at their locations.
choices.D: Scientists who study changes in average sea level rely on many different kinds of data.

candidates.evidence: Long records from tide gauges help scientists track changes in average sea level.
candidates.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs to know what a tide gauge does, and the goal requires why long records matter. Choice A gives both.

B.rationale: This gives one long record but not why such records are valuable.

C.rationale: Reading frequency does not explain the value of long records.

D.rationale: This is vague and does not explain what a tide gauge is.

hints: What must an unfamiliar audience learn?
Which note says why long records matter?

strategy.explanation: List what the goal requires before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Audience and purpose both shape the best answer.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the drink most likely protects people against developing the condition.
choices.B: people with the condition drink the brand more often than other people do.
choices.C: the condition is far more common than researchers had previously thought.
choices.D: the survey offers little evidence that the drink raises the risk of the condition.

candidates.evidence: about 80% of people also report regularly drinking that brand
candidates.explanation: If 80% of everyone drinks the brand, finding that 80% of people with the condition drink it is exactly what chance alone predicts, so the figure gives no evidence of a link.

A.rationale: Equal rates show no association in either direction, not a protective effect.

B.rationale: Both groups report the same 80% rate, so the data show no difference in how often they drink it.

C.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns how common the condition is.

hints: Compare the 80% among patients with the 80% among everyone.
What would you expect if the drink had no effect at all?

strategy.explanation: Predict: the figure is what you'd expect by chance.

candidates.remember: A rate means little without the base rate to compare.
candidates.revision_note: S007-03 resubmitted: relabelled medium (a blind rater judged it easy and noted that A-C were obvious overreaches); choice B replaced with a near-miss that misreads the equal rates.
